Protosilylation
Stable and Recyclable Copper Nanoclusters with Exposed Active
Sites for Broad-Scope Protosilylation in Open Air
Songwei Wen
+
, Chengkai Zhang
+
, Li-Juan Liu, Zhi Wang, Di Sun,* and Jian He*
Abstract: Despite recent advances in cluster-based
catalysis for organic synthesis, the substrate scope of
reactions catalyzed by metal nanoclusters is typically not
superior to previously established catalytic systems.
Herein, we develop new atomically precise copper
nanoclusters for protosilylation, with scope expanding to
alkenes and simple enynes that were not suitable for
prior synthetic methodologies with traditional copper
complexes. The involvement of a second copper center
in the metal kernel during the migratory insertion step is
thought to be responsible for the expanded scope. In
addition, the reaction is highly compatible with water
and can be carried out in open air rather than under
inert gas protection. Mechanistic studies suggest that the
cluster-catalyzed protosilylation proceeds in the absence
of silyl radicals. The current findings demonstrate the
potential of using metal nanoclusters for practical and
sustainable chemical synthesis.
Introduction
Because of the excellent tunability of ligand scaffolds and
kernel structures, as well as the distinct photochemical
characteristics of metal cores, atomically precise metal
nanoclusters have shown promise as effective catalysts for
the development of organic chemical processes.
[1]
In recent
years, considerable efforts have been made toward con-
structing catalytically active copper nanoclusters in gram
scales at low cost for sustainable synthetic applications
[2]
While several types of cluster-catalyzed coupling reactions
can be achieved with increased efficiency,
[3]
developing
robust copper nanocluster catalysts that can significantly
broaden reaction scope when compared to established
catalytic systems based on conventional copper complexes
remains a major challenge.
On account of its flat structure and strong chelating
effects, we anticipated that the incorporation of maleonitri-
ledithiolate (mnt) in cluster synthesis would produce stable
copper nanoclusters with exposed active sites suitable for
practical catalytic applications.
[4]
The presence of Cu � Cu
bonds in nanoclusters could have an important impact on
the elementary steps during catalysis, potentially overcom-
ing synthetic limitations in catalytic organic transformations.
Since protosilylation reactions are crucial for organic
synthesis
[5]
and can be facilitated by copper complexes,
[6]
investigating them with novel copper nanoclusters gave us
an ideal opportunity to test the hypothesis. Even though
copper-catalyzed protosilylation of alkynes and enynes with
(dimethylphenylsilyl)boronic acid pinacol ester (pinB–
SiMe
2
Ph), a readily available and moisture-stable silylboro-
nate, has been extensively studied through the use of various
ligands (Schemes 1a and 1b),
[7]
there is still room for
improvement in terms of catalyst turnover numbers (TONs)
and reaction operability.
Here we report the synthesis and characterization of
copper nanoclusters protected by mnt, thiolate, and bi-
sphosphine ligands, which efficiently catalyze protosilylation
of C � C multiple bonds under air atmosphere (Scheme 1c).
The optimized nanocatalyst can be recycled multiple runs
without loss of reactivity, and its remarkable stability is
further demonstrated by UV–Vis, NMR, and ESI-MS
studies. Aside from the high activity in gram-scale synthesis,
the newly-developed copper nanocluster exhibits outstand-
ing catalytic performance in the protosilylation of alkenes
and enynes without the need for the pre-installation of
electron-withdrawing functionalities.
[7e,8]
Additional interac-
tions between the silyl group and the copper center adjacent
to the exposed active site are likely to promote the key
migratory insertion step, resulting in an expanded substrate
scope in protosilylation reactions.

According to solvent studies, the involvement of protic

Under the optimized reaction conditions, the alkyne
substrates containing a variety of substituted aryl rings
furnish the desired (E)-products with excellent levels of
regioselectivity (Table 2, products 1–11). Both electron-
donating and electron-withdrawing functional groups at
different positions are well tolerated. Apart from phenyl-
acetylene derivatives, alkyl-substituted terminal alkynes
prove to be effective substrates in the protosilylation
(Table 2, products 12 and 13), despite the relatively low
regioselectivity for the substrate with a primary alkyl chain.
Furthermore, under standard conditions, an α,β-unsaturated
ester (14) is obtained with high levels of regio- and stereo-
selectivity. Trimethylsilylacetylene, a commonly used orga-
nosilicon compound, could be converted into a trans-1,2-
disilylethene (15) with 88% yield. In addition, internal
alkyne substrates are highly compatible with the cluster-
based catalytic system (Table 2, products 16–18). Very
importantly, the substrate scope can be further expanded to
alkenes (Table 2, products 19 and 20), which was difficult to
achieve in previous copper catalysis (Figure S5). For the
synthesis of silyl-functionalized allenes, we broadened the
substrate scope from 2-trifluoromethyl enynes to simple
ones (Figure S6), giving desired di-substituted allenes 21 and
22 in yields of 71% and 78%, respectively.
We have expanded our investigation on the functional-
group compatibility of this synthetic method by conducting
the template reaction in the presence of different additives
(Table S7). Across a diverse array of additives such as
aldehydes, ketones, nitriles, and various heterocycles, the
cluster-catalyzed protosilylation proceeded with minimal or
negligible influence on the yield of product 1. While an
aniline displayed some incompatibility, it remained stable
under the reaction conditions. In contrast, although the
protosilylation proceeded effectively in the presence of a
phenol or an N-methyl pyrrole, these two additives exhibited
poor recovery.
Notably, the gram-scale reaction can proceed smoothly
with a 20-fold lower catalyst loading, providing a TON as
high as 14200 (eq. 1). To demonstrate the synthetic utility of
this protosilylation, we subjected product 1 to a range of
coupling and hydrogenation conditions for the construction
of carbon � carbon and carbon–heteroatom bonds
(Scheme 2). A number of functionalized trans-olefins,
including high value-added bromoalkene 26 and diene 28,
were synthesized in high yields. When an electron-deficient
aryl group was introduced to the alkyne terminal of the
enyne, a second protosilylation reaction occurred in the
resulting di-substitute allene,
[13]
activating the double bond
closer to the aromatic ring (eq. 2). The other silyl group
approached the central carbon atom of the allene from the
opposite direction as the previously installed silyl group,
giving disilylated product 33 in the (E)-configuration, most
likely through a migratory insertion pathway.

Since a mixed-solvent strategy was
employed in the reaction optimization, we examined the

Based on the experimental results and DFT calculations,
we proposed a plausible catalytic cycle in Figure 3e. With
the aid of the base and methanol, the exposed active site on
the copper nanocluster undergoes ligand association to
generate cluster–silyl intermediate A. Following the side-on
binding of an alkyne molecule through transition state TS-1,
intermediate B forms with a
t
BuS ligand dissociated from
the copper active center. In the subsequent silyl migration
step, 1,2-insertion occurs with an additional stabilization
effect from the nearby copper center, resulting in the highest
activation energy of only 23.1 kcal mol
–1
. Because of this
unique migratory insertion mode involving two copper
centers of TS-2, the catalytic protosilylation proceeds
smoothly at room temperature, with an extended substrate
scope that includes C = C double bonds. Furthermore, the
concerted insertion leads to the formation of intermediate
C, in which the cluster unit and the silyl group are cis to
each other. Therefore, deprotonation of C with methanol
yields a trans-alkene and intermediate D. The initial cluster
catalyst (Cu
6
-1) is regenerated via ligand dissociation in the
presence of a conjugate acid.
C onclusion
We present here the development of mnt ligand-protected
Cu
6
nanoclusters with exposed active sites for efficiently
catalyzing protosilylation reactions under ambient condi-
tions, with a TON of up to 14200. The nanocatalyst can be
recycled at least 8 runs and is applicable to gram-scale
synthesis. Apart from its high reactivity with alkyne
substrates, the Cu
6
nanocluster can also be employed to
functionalize alkenes and simple enynes. The new migratory
insertion mode based on two copper centers in the cluster
kernel provides guidance for the future design of catalyti-
cally active metal nanoclusters to transform synthetic
methodologies.

Protosilylation

Stable and Recyclable Copper Nanoclusters with Exposed Active
Sites for Broad-Scope Protosilylation in Open Air
Songwei Wen<sup>+</sup>, Chengkai Zhang<sup>+</sup>, Li-Juan Liu, Zhi Wang, Di Sun,* and Jian He*

Abstract: Despite recent advances in cluster-based
catalysis for organic synthesis, the substrate scope of
reactions catalyzed by metal nanoclusters is typically not
superior to previously established catalytic systems.
Herein, we develop new atomically precise copper
nanoclusters for protosilylation, with scope expanding to
alkenes and simple enynes that were not suitable for
prior synthetic methodologies with traditional copper
complexes. The involvement of a second copper center
in the metal kernel during the migratory insertion step is
thought to be responsible for the expanded scope. In
addition, the reaction is highly compatible with water
and can be carried out in open air rather than under
inert gas protection. Mechanistic studies suggest that the
cluster-catalyzed protosilylation proceeds in the absence
of silyl radicals. The current findings demonstrate the
potential of using metal nanoclusters for practical and
sustainable chemical synthesis.
Introduction

Because of the excellent tunability of ligand scaffolds and
kernel structures, as well as the distinct photochemical
characteristics of metal cores, atomically precise metal
nanoclusters have shown promise as effective catalysts for
the development of organic chemical processes.<sup>[1]</sup> In recent
years, considerable efforts have been made toward con-
structing catalytically active copper nanoclusters in gram
scales at low cost for sustainable synthetic applications<sup>[2]</sup>
While several types of cluster-catalyzed coupling reactions

can be achieved with increased efficiency,<sup>[3]</sup> developing
robust copper nanocluster catalysts that can significantly
broaden reaction scope when compared to established
catalytic systems based on conventional copper complexes
remains a major challenge.

On account of its flat structure and strong chelating
effects, we anticipated that the incorporation of maleonitri-
ledithiolate (mnt) in cluster synthesis would produce stable
copper nanoclusters with exposed active sites suitable for
practical catalytic applications.<sup>[4]</sup> The presence of Cu�Cu
bonds in nanoclusters could have an important impact on
the elementary steps during catalysis, potentially overcom-
ing synthetic limitations in catalytic organic transformations.
Since protosilylation reactions are crucial for organic
synthesis<sup>[5]</sup> and can be facilitated by copper complexes,<sup>[6]</sup>
investigating them with novel copper nanoclusters gave us
an ideal opportunity to test the hypothesis. Even though
copper-catalyzed protosilylation of alkynes and enynes with
(dimethylphenylsilyl)boronic acid pinacol ester (pinB–
SiMe Ph), a readily available and moisture-stable silylboro-
nate, has been extensively studied through the use of various
ligands (Schemes 1a and 1b),<sup>[7]</sup> there is still room for
improvement in terms of catalyst turnover numbers (TONs)
and reaction operability.

Here we report the synthesis and characterization of
copper nanoclusters protected by mnt, thiolate, and bi-
sphosphine ligands, which efficiently catalyze protosilylation
of C�C multiple bonds under air atmosphere (Scheme 1c).
The optimized nanocatalyst can be recycled multiple runs
without loss of reactivity, and its remarkable stability is
further demonstrated by UV–Vis, NMR, and ESI-MS
studies. Aside from the high activity in gram-scale synthesis,
the newly-developed copper nanocluster exhibits outstand-
ing catalytic performance in the protosilylation of alkenes
and enynes without the need for the pre-installation of
electron-withdrawing functionalities.<sup>[7e,8]</sup> Additional interac-
tions between the silyl group and the copper center adjacent
to the exposed active site are likely to promote the key
migratory insertion step, resulting in an expanded substrate
scope in protosilylation reactions.

cluster-catalyzed protosilylation proceeded with minimal or
negligible influence on the yield of product 1. While an
aniline displayed some incompatibility, it remained stable
under the reaction conditions. In contrast, although the
protosilylation proceeded effectively in the presence of a
phenol or an N-methyl pyrrole, these two additives exhibited
poor recovery.

Notably, the gram-scale reaction can proceed smoothly
with a 20-fold lower catalyst loading, providing a TON as
high as 14200 (eq. 1). To demonstrate the synthetic utility of
this protosilylation, we subjected product 1 to a range of
coupling and hydrogenation conditions for the construction
of carbon�carbon and carbon–heteroatom bonds
(Scheme 2). A number of functionalized trans-olefins,
including high value-added bromoalkene 26 and diene 28,
were synthesized in high yields. When an electron-deficient
aryl group was introduced to the alkyne terminal of the

resulting di-substitute allene,<sup>[13]</sup> activating the double bond
closer to the aromatic ring (eq. 2). The other silyl group
approached the central carbon atom of the allene from the
opposite direction as the previously installed silyl group,
giving disilylated product 33 in the (E)-configuration, most
likely through a migratory insertion pathway.

Based on the experimental results and DFT calculations,
we proposed a plausible catalytic cycle in Figure 3e. With
the aid of the base and methanol, the exposed active site on
the copper nanocluster undergoes ligand association to
generate cluster–silyl intermediate A. Following the side-on
binding of an alkyne molecule through transition state TS-1,
intermediate B forms with a <sup>t</sup>BuS ligand dissociated from
the copper active center. In the subsequent silyl migration
step, 1,2-insertion occurs with an additional stabilization
effect from the nearby copper center, resulting in the highest
activation energy of only 23.1 kcal mol<sup>–1</sup>. Because of this
unique migratory insertion mode involving two copper
centers of TS-2, the catalytic protosilylation proceeds
smoothly at room temperature, with an extended substrate
scope that includes
\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { C }
double bonds. Furthermore, the
concerted insertion leads to the formation of intermediate
\mathbf { C } ,
in which the cluster unit and the silyl group are cis to
each other. Therefore, deprotonation of C with methanol
yields a trans-alkene and intermediate D. The initial cluster
catalyst
\bf ( C u _ { 6 } – 1 )
is regenerated via ligand dissociation in the
presence of a conjugate acid.
Conclusion

We present here the development of mnt ligand-protected
\mathrm { C u } _ { 6 }
nanoclusters with exposed active sites for efficiently
catalyzing protosilylation reactions under ambient condi-
tions, with a TON of up to 14200. The nanocatalyst can be
recycled at least 8 runs and is applicable to gram-scale
synthesis. Apart from its high reactivity with alkyne
substrates, the
\mathrm { C u } _ { 6 }
nanocluster can also be employed to
functionalize alkenes and simple enynes. The new migratory
insertion mode based on two copper centers in the cluster
kernel provides guidance for the future design of catalyti-
cally active metal nanoclusters to transform synthetic
methodologies.
